title: Practice workshop
intro: Bring the handbook into one real situation: understand it, choose an action, keep a record, and revise your judgment in light of the result.

ui.eyebrow: Dual Quotient Manual · Room to grow
ui.growing: Start with three modules, with more cases, tools and topics to come. Choose just one problem that matters to you today.
ui.casesIntro: Choose a response first, then consider its benefits, costs and conditions.
ui.workbookIntro: Write down decisions, emotions, conversations and boundaries so you can revisit them.
ui.topicsIntro: Consider people's needs alongside resources, rules, decision authority and costs.
ui.caseNote: These fictional cases draw on common situations. With incomplete information, several responses may be reasonable. Explore trade-offs rather than receiving a personality score.
ui.chooseFirst: Choose a response to see what it might resolve and what it might leave unresolved.
ui.privacy: Your writing stays in this browser and is not uploaded. All languages share the same records; your original words stay unchanged. Export a backup before changing devices or clearing browser data.
ui.draftHelp: Each worksheet has its own automatically saved draft. Save a record to keep a snapshot of your thinking; you can then continue editing the draft.
ui.draftSaved: Drafts are saved automatically in this browser.

ui.nextBody: End each exercise with one observable action and a review date. When you return, compare your earlier judgment with what happened. New cases and topics will continue to be added here.

cases.title: A client adds a last-minute request
cases.situation: Two days before delivery, a client asks for an extra feature they say should be simple, within the original deadline. You have not estimated the work, and the team's schedule is full.
cases.question: How would you respond?

options.text: Agree first, then ask the team to work overtime.
options.feedback: This eases immediate pressure but turns unknown effort into a promise at the team's expense. A commitment needs a verified estimate, resources and authority.

options.text: Say it is out of scope and refuse all changes.
options.feedback: This protects scope but may miss a genuinely urgent need. Explain any firm constraints; otherwise discuss replacing scope or changing the date.

options.text: Clarify the need, then offer scope, timing and resource options.
options.feedback: This makes the trade-offs clear, but set a deadline for the estimate so that checking does not become delay. Have the authorized person confirm the choice.

cases.principle: Understanding a client's urgency does not require making unverified commitments. The requester, approver and person bearing the cost may be different people.
cases.action: Try: I will check the impact and provide two options this afternoon: keep the date and change the scope, or keep the scope and change the date. Please then confirm your priority.
cases.review: Was the extra scope clear? Who approved the decision? Were the costs to timing, quality and working hours visible?

cases.title: Being criticized in a meeting
cases.situation: During a discussion, a colleague says, “You never think things through.” You feel embarrassed and do not know which risk they mean.
cases.question: What would you say next?

options.text: Point out mistakes they have made in the past.
options.feedback: This may briefly protect your pride, but it turns a discussion of the plan into a personal conflict. The factual issue remains unresolved, and others may find it harder to contribute.

options.text: Accept everything to end the discussion quickly.
options.feedback: This can reduce tension, but you may accept an inaccurate generalization without learning what needs correcting. Check the facts once things settle.

options.text: Ask for the specific omission and separate the person from the plan.
options.feedback: This can restore a factual discussion: Which assumption do you mean? Repeated belittling may also require a separate conversation about boundaries.

cases.principle: Separate specific behavior and risks from broad judgments about a person. Accepting useful information does not mean accepting humiliating language.
cases.action: Ask: Please identify the omission so we can check it. Later, say privately: I welcome feedback on the plan and would like us to avoid generalizations such as “you always.”
cases.review: What verifiable omission did you find? Did you express a boundary? Did the next interaction change?

cases.title: You know the deadline will be missed
cases.situation: Your task is blocked and now looks likely to finish three days late. You worry that reporting it will make you look incapable, so you want to find a solution before saying anything.
cases.question: How will you handle the bad news?

options.text: Stay quiet and hope to catch up at the last moment.
options.feedback: This protects appearances briefly but leaves others less time to adjust. If delivery is still late, the problem becomes a risk to both the schedule and trust.

options.text: Promise an even tighter new date to reassure everyone.
options.feedback: This may comfort people briefly, but without evidence that the blocker can be removed, it only postpones uncertainty. New commitments need resources and scope to support them.

options.text: Report the known facts, unknowns and possible remedies early.
options.feedback: This exposes the difficulty but gives the team room to adapt. Distinguish confirmed effects from estimates and agree when you will update them next.

cases.principle: Taking responsibility includes giving affected people timely information they can act on. Reporting a risk is different from shifting blame.
cases.action: Write a short update: work completed, blocker, expected impact, who needs to do what, and the next checkpoint.
cases.review: Was the warning early enough? Which assumptions proved wrong? What signal could you notice sooner next time?

cases.title: Your contribution was left out
cases.situation: A colleague presents a shared achievement without mentioning your key contribution. You feel they took the credit, but do not yet know whether it was intentional.
cases.question: What would you do first?

options.text: Accuse them of stealing credit in the group chat.
options.feedback: This makes your frustration visible but may escalate conflict before the evidence is clear. Separate a verifiable omission from a guess about motives.

options.text: Say nothing and hope they notice next time.
options.feedback: This avoids immediate friction but may leave them unaware of the issue. If attribution affects evaluation, continued silence leaves the same rules in place.

options.text: Check privately, then request a specific correction.
options.feedback: This leaves room for an honest omission while asking for an observable change. If repeated conversations fail, bring the facts to the person responsible for contribution records.

cases.principle: Establish facts before interpreting motives and incentives. Address both this omission and how the team records and recognizes work.
cases.action: List the shared result, each person's work and existing evidence. Ask for a specific acknowledgment in the next update.
cases.review: Was the attribution corrected? Is future recordkeeping clear? Do you have more evidence about intent?

cases.title: They want to be heard; you offer solutions
cases.situation: A family member says they have had an exhausting day. You immediately suggest fixes, and they say, “You are not listening.” You feel your good intentions were misunderstood.
cases.question: How could you respond now?

options.text: Explain why your advice is correct.
options.feedback: This adds reasoning but may still miss their immediate need. Whether advice is useful and whether someone is ready for it are separate questions.

options.text: Decide never to offer an opinion again.
options.feedback: This avoids another disappointment for now but turns a mismatch in one conversation into withdrawal. Ask what kind of support they want.

options.text: Reflect what you heard, then ask whether they want listening or ideas.
options.feedback: This lets them choose the support they need. If you also lack energy, honestly agree on a time when you can listen properly.

cases.principle: Check what help the other person wants. Your wish to solve a problem does not automatically mean they want a plan.
cases.action: Try: It sounds like you have been holding everything together today. Would you like me to listen first, or think through the next step with you?
cases.review: How did they describe their need? Did you reflect it accurately? Was advice offered after an invitation?

cases.title: Helping others is taking all your time
cases.situation: A friend often asks for help at short notice. You find it hard to refuse, but it is affecting your sleep and plans. You agree while becoming increasingly resentful.
cases.question: How will you answer this request?

options.text: Keep agreeing and hope they realize you are tired.
options.feedback: This maintains surface harmony but gives no clear boundary. They may interpret your repeated agreement as spare capacity.

options.text: List every past grievance and say you will never help again.
options.feedback: This stops the burden quickly, but accumulated frustration can become a sweeping accusation. If there is no safety concern, first state clear limits for this request and future ones.

options.text: Explain what you cannot do and offer only help you can deliver.
options.feedback: They may be disappointed, but the relationship rests on real capacity. Alternatives are optional; you need not take on the same burden to prove goodwill.

cases.principle: Understanding someone's difficulty does not make solving it your responsibility. A boundary describes your actions, not what someone else must think.
cases.action: Try: I cannot take this on this week. I can spend fifteen minutes on it on Saturday. If that is not enough, you will need another arrangement.
cases.review: Did you uphold your limit? Did guilt lead you to add more? Can the other person respect a clear refusal?

cases.title: The team cannot choose between two plans
cases.situation: Both plans have supporters. People keep repeating advantages, disagree about the risks and have not agreed who will make the final decision.
cases.question: How would you move the discussion forward?

options.text: Find more arguments proving your side is right.
options.feedback: This may add evidence or simply repeat a position. First check whether both sides share a goal and decision criteria.

options.text: Vote immediately and let the majority decide.
options.feedback: This works when voting is agreed and appropriate to the consequences. If a minority bears the risks or responsibility is unclear, votes cannot replace authority and evidence.

options.text: Agree on criteria and decision authority, then design a small reversible trial.
options.feedback: This turns debate into observable comparison. Set a time limit, cost ceiling and results that would change the choice, or the trial itself may drift indefinitely.

cases.principle: Separate disagreements about values from disagreements about facts. The former require an accountable decision; information or small trials may narrow the latter.
cases.action: Each person writes the goal, the failure they most fear and the evidence that would change their mind. Then agree on a time-limited check.
cases.review: Which evidence changed the choice? Who owned the decision? Did the trial stop or expand as agreed?

cases.title: Should you continue after investing so much?
cases.situation: You have spent two months on a plan, but its central assumption remains untested. Continuing still seems hopeful; stopping feels like wasting all your effort.
cases.question: How will you decide what comes next?

options.text: Insist on finishing because you have already invested so much.
options.feedback: Wanting to honor your effort is understandable, but time already spent does not prove the next step is worthwhile. Compare future benefits, costs and alternatives.

options.text: Give up as soon as difficulty appears.
options.feedback: This avoids further expenditure but may mean leaving a solvable problem too soon. Distinguish a temporary obstacle from a disproven core assumption.

options.text: Reassess future value and set limits on one final test.
options.feedback: This makes both continuing and stopping depend on observable conditions. The test is useful only if it can provide new information at an acceptable cost.

cases.principle: Acknowledge disappointment, then assess the next step. You can value what you learned while stopping a plan that no longer merits more effort.
cases.action: Write what new evidence another week could bring, how much more you will invest, and which result would make you stop or change direction.
cases.review: Did you respect the stopping rule? If you changed it, was that due to new information or greater difficulty admitting a loss?

templates.title: Decision journal
templates.description: Record your reasoning before acting, then compare it with the result.

fields.label: The decision
fields.hint: State the specific question, deadline and confirmed facts.

fields.label: Available options
fields.hint: Write at least two options, including postponement if relevant, with benefits and costs.

fields.label: Evidence and uncertainty
fields.hint: What am I relying on? What information is missing? What counterexample would change my mind?

fields.label: Choice and expectation
fields.hint: What do I choose, and why? What do I expect? If using a probability, specify the event it refers to.

fields.label: Action and stopping conditions
fields.hint: Who will do what, and when? What is the limit on effort? Which signal means pause or adjust?

fields.label: Review date and outcome
fields.hint: Set a review date first. Later, record the outcome and distinguish the quality of your judgment from luck.

templates.title: Emotion journal
templates.description: Separate facts, interpretations and needs to find a response you can choose.

fields.label: What happened
fields.hint: Describe events as a camera would, without guessing motives yet.

fields.label: Emotions and physical signals
fields.hint: Name the emotion as specifically as possible. You can also record intensity and physical sensations.

fields.label: My interpretation
fields.hint: What judgment came to mind? What other explanation is plausible?

fields.label: What matters and what I need
fields.hint: What am I trying to protect? Which needs can I meet myself, and which call for a request?

fields.label: Possible responses
fields.hint: Pause, clarify, ask, decline or leave? Choose an action you can actually take.

fields.label: Review and adjustment
fields.hint: When will I review this? What happened after I acted? What would I keep or change next time?

templates.title: Difficult conversation planner
templates.description: Turn what you want to say into a specific, clear request someone can respond to.

fields.label: Event and conversation goal
fields.hint: What happened specifically? What one issue should this conversation resolve?

fields.label: What each person may care about
fields.hint: Separate confirmed information from guesses. Prepare a question to check your understanding.

fields.label: My opening words
fields.hint: Describe behavior, impact and your needs. Avoid “you always” and labels about the person.

fields.label: Specific request and options
fields.hint: Who should do what, by when? If that is not possible, what alternatives exist?

fields.label: Boundaries and exit plan
fields.hint: What language or requests are unacceptable? If they recur, will I pause or take another action?

fields.label: Agreement and review
fields.hint: What did each person actually agree to? When will you check progress? What remains unresolved?

templates.title: Interests and boundaries map
templates.description: Identify participants, incentives, costs and what you can decide.

fields.label: Shared problem and goal
fields.hint: Are all parties addressing the same issue? What would resolution look like?

fields.label: People and needs
fields.hint: Who requests, decides, acts and is affected? What does each person want to gain or avoid?

fields.label: Rules and incentives
fields.hint: What behavior is rewarded or penalized? Who pays the costs and who benefits? What is still only a guess?

fields.label: Resources, information and authority
fields.hint: Who holds key resources and information? What can I decide, and whose approval do I need?

fields.label: Negotiable points and limits
fields.hint: What can be traded, and what needs a clear refusal? How will I act if a limit is crossed?

fields.label: Proposal and validation
fields.hint: State a concrete proposal, owner and review date. What feedback would show that it works?

topics.title: Needs behind positions
topics.idea: “It must be delivered today” is a position. Behind it may be a promise, an evaluation, a worry or a real use date. Treat these as hypotheses to check, not conclusions about motives.
questions: What does the other person want to gain or avoid?
Which part of the request is least flexible?
Would they discuss another way to meet the need?
topics.example: Someone needs a full report by Friday. On checking, the Friday meeting needs only three conclusions. You can offer a summary first and agree a separate date for the full report.
topics.boundary: People may be unable or unwilling to explain every need. Keep checking facts rather than telling them what they “really” want.

topics.title: Incentives behind behavior
topics.idea: Repeated behavior may relate to rewards, penalties and who bears costs. Appeals to attitude alone may not change an arrangement that makes the wrong behavior pay.
questions: Which behavior gets recognized most easily now?
Who pays extra for doing the right thing?
How could responsibility, resources and evaluation align better?
topics.example: A team is assessed only by task count, so complex work is avoided. Alongside encouraging responsibility, discuss difficulty, quality and collaborative contributions.
topics.boundary: Incentives are one possible explanation. Skills, information, resources or temporary pressures may produce the same behavior; compare the evidence.

topics.title: Participation, influence and decision authority
topics.idea: Advising, executing and approving changes are different roles. Giving responsibility without resources or authority can produce apparent agreement that cannot be delivered.
questions: Who can approve changes to scope, dates or resources?
Who bears the consequences of the decision?
Does the person doing the work have the information and support they need?
topics.example: A client contact requests extra work, but another owner must approve the budget. Have the right person confirm the trade-offs before making promises to the delivery team.
topics.boundary: Clear decision authority does not mean ignoring affected people. Even in urgent situations, record temporary decisions and obtain confirmation promptly.

topics.title: Turn disputes into negotiable options
topics.idea: Break an all-or-nothing dispute into scope, timing, quality, resources and responsibility. Some constraints can be traded; others require acknowledging that you cannot have everything.
questions: What matters most to each side?
What can I change, and who bears the cost?
What small, reversible step could test an option?
topics.example: When asked to add features and deliver earlier, offer a smaller first release, confirmed additional resources or two deliveries. Make the costs of each choice visible.
topics.boundary: Not everything is a transaction. Do not obscure respect, safety or basic commitments with vague trades, or offer options you have no authority to deliver.

topics.title: Boundaries are commitments about your own actions
topics.idea: A boundary states what you will do under particular conditions. It allows others their choices while clarifying what you will not take on indefinitely.
questions: Which specific behaviors can I accept, and which can I not?
If this happens again, what action can I actually take?
Am I mixing requests, expectations and firm limits?
topics.example: “Please do not message me late at night” is a request. “After 8 p.m., I will reply the next day; use the agreed channel for urgent matters” states your own action boundary.
topics.boundary: Boundaries should account for actual duties and commitments. In threatening or persistently harmful situations, prioritize getting to safety and seeking appropriate support; endurance is not the exercise.

topics.title: When to talk, escalate or leave
topics.idea: A misunderstanding may need clarification; repeated broken agreements may call for different cooperation rules. More explanation cannot always fix missing resources, authority or safety.
questions: Does the same issue recur despite clear agreements?
Is the gap information, ability, resources or willingness to honor a commitment?
Who should intervene next, or under what conditions should cooperation stop?
topics.example: Required materials remain missing after several agreements. Summarize requests, dates and impacts for the responsible person; if necessary, pause affected work under the agreed conditions.
topics.boundary: Escalate around facts, impacts and decisions needed, rather than punishment or winning. Explain exit conditions in advance where possible, and address actual safety risks promptly.
